category.name: Domain & Infrastructure
category.description: Tools for mapping the technical footprint behind a domain, host or netblock: DNS, certificates, passive DNS history, exposed services and subdomains. This is where most investigations into a website, a phishing kit or an anonymous operator begin.

tools.name: Shodan
tools.summary: Search engine for internet-connected hosts and services, indexed by banner, port, protocol and location.
tools.description:
Shodan continuously scans the public IPv4 space and records what answers on each port: service banners, TLS certificates, HTTP headers, favicon hashes, industrial control protocols. You query it the way you query a search engine, but the corpus is infrastructure rather than pages.

In an investigation it is used to pivot. Given one server you can find every other host presenting the same certificate, the same self-signed CA, the same favicon or the same unusual banner string — which is often how a cluster of related infrastructure is discovered behind different domains. It is also the standard way to check whether an organisation has exposed something it did not mean to expose.

Limits: Shodan sees only what responds to its scanners, and its data is as old as its last crawl of that host — a result is evidence of a past state, not the present one. Hosts behind CDNs, firewalls that drop unsolicited traffic, or IPv6-only deployments are largely invisible. Always confirm a Shodan hit against a live check before asserting it.
tools.costNotes: A free registered account gives limited search with reduced filters and result counts. Broader search, filters and export require a paid membership; API access is sold separately, and there are enterprise tiers. Shodan has historically run heavily discounted lifetime-membership promotions. Exact current prices were not confirmed during this review — check the store page before budgeting.
tools.legalNotes: Querying Shodan's index is passive: you are searching a database Shodan already collected, not touching the target, so the subject is not notified. Acting on results is where risk begins — connecting to, authenticating against or probing a discovered host is an active act that can engage the CFAA, the UK Computer Misuse Act or equivalent. Never use a found credential or default login. Redistribution of bulk Shodan data is restricted by its terms.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Coverage of common ports and protocols is broad and the data model is stable. Freshness varies by host — a banner may be weeks old. Geolocation of IPs is inherited from third-party geo databases and is frequently wrong at city level. Treat every record as 'observed at timestamp X', never as current state.
tools.confidenceNotes: Homepage fetched and confirmed live during this review; pricing detail deliberately left qualitative because tier prices were not confirmed from the primary pricing page.

tools.name: Censys Search
tools.summary: Internet-wide host and certificate scanning with a strong certificate corpus and structured query language.
tools.description:
Censys scans the public internet and publishes structured records for hosts and X.509 certificates. Its certificate dataset is the reason most investigators keep it alongside Shodan: you can search certificates by subject, issuer, fingerprint or SAN entry and find every host that ever presented them.

Typical use is certificate-led pivoting. An operator who reuses a TLS certificate, a distinctive Subject Organisation string, or a self-signed CA across nominally unrelated domains links them for you. Censys's query language supports field-level filters, which makes it better than Shodan for precise structured queries and worse for casual keyword browsing.

Limits: the same 'observed at a point in time' caveat applies. Censys retired its legacy Search product for free users after 31 March 2025 and moved everyone to the newer Censys Platform; older tutorials and saved queries written for legacy Search will not work.
tools.costNotes: A free registered tier exists on the Censys Platform. During 2025 Censys expanded what free users get, adding asset-lookup API access, one collection of up to 100 assets, and standard plus advanced protocol data in both UI and API. Paid tiers add volume, history and export. Legacy Search was deprecated for free users after 31 March 2025.
tools.legalNotes: Passive lookup against Censys's own index; the subject is not notified. Bulk export and redistribution are governed by the Censys terms and differ sharply between free and commercial use — read them before putting Censys data into a published dataset or a commercial product.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Certificate data is high quality and well structured. Host data is a scan snapshot with the usual freshness caveats. The 2025 platform migration means answers found in third-party guides may reference fields or endpoints that no longer exist.
tools.confidenceNotes: Free-tier changes and the legacy-Search deprecation date confirmed against Censys documentation and product announcements during this review.

tools.name: crt.sh
tools.summary: Free searchable interface to public Certificate Transparency logs, operated by Sectigo.
tools.description:
Every publicly trusted TLS certificate issued since Certificate Transparency became mandatory is logged to append-only public logs. crt.sh indexes those logs and lets you search them by domain, organisation, or certificate identifier without an account.

Its single most valuable use is subdomain discovery. A wildcard search such as `%.example.com` returns every hostname that has ever appeared in a certificate for that domain — including staging, admin, VPN and internal-sounding hosts that nobody intended to publish. Because CT is append-only, it is also a historical record: you can see when a subdomain first appeared, which is useful for dating an operation.

Limits: CT only covers publicly trusted certificates. Internal CAs, self-signed certificates and hosts that never got a public certificate will not appear. A hostname in CT is not proof the host exists or ever resolved — certificates get issued for names that are never deployed.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account, no advertised query cost. There is no formal SLA; it is a public-good service operated by Sectigo.
tools.legalNotes: Certificate Transparency logs are public by design and searching them is unambiguously lawful. No notification reaches the certificate holder. The data can nonetheless reveal an organisation's internal naming, so handle findings about a private party with the same care as any other sensitive disclosure.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The underlying CT data is authoritative — it is the log, not an interpretation of it. The service itself is known for intermittent unavailability and gateway errors under load; a 502 was observed during this review. If crt.sh is down, the same CT data is reachable through other CT search front-ends and through the logs directly. Presence of a hostname in CT does not imply the host resolves.
tools.confidenceNotes: Checked during this review. The site returned an HTTP 502 at the moment of checking, which is consistent with its well-documented intermittent availability rather than evidence of shutdown; the service and its operator are otherwise unchanged.

tools.name: DNSDumpster
tools.summary: Free DNS reconnaissance showing records, subdomains and hosting relationships for a domain.
tools.description:
DNSDumpster, run by HackerTarget, resolves a domain and presents its DNS surface in one view: A, MX, NS and TXT records, discovered subdomains, and the hosting netblocks they sit in. It is the fastest way to get an orienting picture of a domain before deciding where to dig.

Investigators use it as a first pass — it takes seconds and tells you whether a domain is on shared hosting, behind a CDN, using a mail provider that reveals something, or sitting alongside other names on the same small netblock. That last case is the interesting one: a lone server hosting several thematically related domains is a strong lead.

Limits: subdomain discovery is not exhaustive and is weaker than a dedicated enumeration run with Amass or Subfinder plus CT logs. Treat it as orientation, not coverage.
tools.costNotes: Free use is available. A free membership account raises limits — reported as roughly 50 queries per day with a 50-result cap per request and API access to records — and a paid Plus membership raises them further. Exact current limits should be checked on the membership page before relying on them.
tools.legalNotes: DNS lookups are ordinary public queries. Note that unlike a purely index-based service, resolution-based reconnaissance touches public DNS infrastructure; this is routine and lawful, but a very large automated run against one domain is a footprint. The target does not receive notification of a DNSDumpster query.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Accurate on the records it returns, but subdomain coverage is partial and result caps on the free tier silently truncate. Never state 'the domain has N subdomains' on DNSDumpster output alone.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed live with a free tier and membership-based limits during this review; the specific numeric limits come from the operator's own membership and developer pages as summarised in search results rather than a direct primary fetch, so they are stated as approximate.

tools.name: urlscan.io
tools.summary: Sandbox that loads a URL in an instrumented browser and records every request, redirect, resource and screenshot.
tools.description:
urlscan.io visits a URL on your behalf from its own infrastructure and produces a full record of what happened: the DOM, a screenshot, every outbound request, the redirect chain, the certificates, the IPs and ASNs contacted, and any third-party trackers or scripts loaded. It also maintains a searchable archive of every public scan ever run.

This matters twice over. First, you can inspect a hostile page — a phishing kit, a malware dropper, a scam storefront — without loading it in your own browser or revealing your IP. Second, the archive is a research corpus: you can search historical scans for a distinctive script, a favicon hash, a form action, or a domain, and find every other page that shared it. That is one of the most effective ways to map a phishing campaign.

Limits and a serious caveat: scans default to a visibility level, and public scans are permanently searchable by anyone, including the operator of the page you scanned. Analysts have leaked internal URLs and sensitive tokens this way. Choose the visibility deliberately every time.
tools.costNotes: Free scanning and search are available, including without an account for basic public scans. Unlisted and private scan visibility, higher rate limits, retention and full search capability sit behind registered and paid tiers. Operated commercially by urlscan GmbH.
tools.legalNotes: urlscan fetches the target page from its own infrastructure, so the request appears in the target's logs as coming from urlscan, not you — but it does appear. This is an active retrieval, not a passive index lookup, and a vigilant operator can see they were scanned and correlate the timing. Critically: a public scan is published. Never scan a URL containing a session token, a password-reset link, an invite link or an internal hostname on public visibility. Doing so has repeatedly caused real credential exposure.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The capture is a faithful record of one fetch from one vantage point at one time. Cloaking is common in malicious infrastructure: a page may serve benign content to urlscan's known ranges and hostile content to real victims, so a clean scan is weak evidence of a clean site. Re-scan from different settings before concluding anything is benign.
tools.confidenceNotes: Homepage fetched during this review, live, operated by urlscan GmbH. Exact tier boundaries were not read from the pricing page and are described qualitatively.

tools.name: SecurityTrails
tools.summary: Historical DNS and WHOIS data — what a domain's records used to say, not just what they say now.
tools.description:
SecurityTrails' distinguishing asset is history. It keeps time series of DNS records and WHOIS registrant data, so you can ask what a domain's A record pointed at two years ago, or who was listed as registrant before privacy protection was switched on.

That historical WHOIS is the single most common way an anonymised domain is attributed. Operators frequently register a domain with real details, then enable privacy later; the original record persists in historical datasets. Reverse lookups — every domain that ever resolved to this IP, every domain registered to this email or name server — turn one identifier into a cluster.

SecurityTrails was acquired by Recorded Future in January 2022 for a reported $65 million and now sits inside that portfolio, which has progressively pulled capability toward the commercial platform. Free-tier generosity has declined over time.
tools.costNotes: A limited free account tier has historically existed with a small monthly API and query allowance; substantive use, reverse lookups at volume and API access are paid. Since the Recorded Future acquisition the commercial offering has been the focus. Current free-tier limits were not confirmed against the primary pricing page during this review — verify before relying on free access.
tools.legalNotes: Passive index lookup; the domain owner is not notified. Historical WHOIS contains personal data of registrants, including natural persons — under GDPR that is personal data you are processing, and a journalistic or legitimate-interest basis needs to be genuine, documented and proportionate. Publishing a registrant's home address obtained this way is a distinct and higher-risk decision from using it as a lead.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Historical records are generally accurate for what was observed, but coverage has gaps, especially for domains outside major TLDs and for periods before their collection began. Absence of a historical record is not evidence the record never existed. Registrant data can also be deliberately falsified at registration, so a name in historical WHOIS is a lead requiring corroboration, never an identification.
tools.confidenceNotes: Recorded Future's acquisition of SecurityTrails (January 2022, reported $65M) confirmed during this review. Current free-tier limits are not confirmed and are described only qualitatively.

tools.name: ViewDNS.info
tools.summary: Free browser-based collection of DNS, WHOIS, reverse-IP and propagation lookups in one place.
tools.description:
ViewDNS.info bundles a few dozen small network lookups behind one page: reverse IP (what else is on this host), reverse WHOIS, reverse NS, DNS propagation checks, port checks, IP history and traceroute.

It is not deep, and none of these tools are unique to it. Its value is speed and the absence of friction — no account, no install, and a set of pivots that would otherwise take several separate services. Reverse IP is the one most used in practice, for the same reason as with DNSDumpster: shared infrastructure links otherwise unconnected domains.

Limits: reverse-IP results on large shared hosting are noise, because thousands of unrelated sites share the address. The free lookups are rate-limited and the underlying datasets are less complete than dedicated commercial passive-DNS providers.
tools.costNotes: The web lookups are free with rate limiting and no account. A paid API is offered for programmatic access. Specific pricing was not confirmed in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Ordinary public network lookups; no subject notification. Reverse WHOIS surfaces personal data of registrants — the same data-protection caution as any WHOIS source applies.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Useful as a quick pivot, weaker than dedicated passive-DNS providers on completeness and freshness. Reverse-IP output is close to meaningless on shared hosting and behind CDNs. Corroborate any link it suggests before treating it as a relationship.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established free lookup service, stable for many years. Not fetched during this review; API pricing unconfirmed.

tools.name: OWASP Amass
tools.summary: Open-source attack-surface mapping that combines dozens of passive sources with optional active enumeration.
tools.description:
Amass is the most thorough open-source tool for enumerating an organisation's external DNS footprint. It queries a long list of passive sources — certificate transparency, passive DNS providers, search engines, threat-intel feeds, WHOIS — and can optionally add active techniques such as brute-force name guessing and zone transfers.

It is run from the command line and maintains a local graph database, so results accumulate across runs and can be diffed over time. That makes it suitable for monitoring: run it monthly and you see when new infrastructure appears.

The critical distinction for an investigator is passive versus active mode. Passive mode only queries third-party datasets and never touches the target. Active mode resolves and probes the target directly. These are legally and operationally different acts and Amass will happily do both, so know which flags you are running.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source under an OWASP project licence. Some of the third-party data sources it can query require your own API keys, and several of those sources are themselves paid — Amass is free but a fully configured Amass is not necessarily.
tools.legalNotes: Passive mode is index querying and carries the usual low risk. Active mode — brute-force subdomain resolution, zone-transfer attempts, port probing — generates traffic to the target and appears in its logs. Depending on jurisdiction and intent this can constitute unauthorised probing; in the UK the Computer Misuse Act and in the US the CFAA are the relevant exposures. Do not run active enumeration against infrastructure you have no authorisation to test.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Best-in-class recall for open tooling when properly configured with API keys; poorly configured it silently returns much less. Results include stale and never-resolving names harvested from historical sources, so every discovered host needs a live resolution check before it goes in a finding.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-running, widely used OWASP project. Not fetched during this review; the project has changed maintainers and major versions over its life, so confirm the current repository and flag syntax before scripting against it.

tools.name: theHarvester
tools.summary: Open-source collector that gathers emails, subdomains, hosts and names for a domain from public sources.
tools.description:
theHarvester queries search engines, certificate transparency, PGP key servers and a range of OSINT APIs to assemble what is publicly discoverable about a domain: email addresses, hostnames, employee names, IPs and open ports where a source provides them.

It is a standard early step in both red-team reconnaissance and journalistic mapping of an organisation. The output is a starting inventory rather than an answer — its job is to tell you what exists so you know what to investigate.

Limits: it depends entirely on the sources it can reach, many of which now require API keys or have tightened rate limits, so results vary widely between installations and over time. Harvested email addresses are frequently stale, guessed by third-party services, or pattern-generated rather than observed.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source. Many of its most productive modules require your own API keys for third-party services, some of which are paid.
tools.legalNotes: Collection is via third-party sources rather than direct contact with the target in most modules, but some modules do perform DNS resolution or host checks. Collected email addresses are personal data under GDPR the moment you store them; a compiled list of an organisation's staff emails is a dataset with real obligations attached, and it should not be retained longer than the investigation needs it.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Highly variable by configuration and by the current state of its upstream sources. Email results in particular include a high proportion of false positives from pattern-guessing services. Verify any address before relying on it and never assume a harvested address is currently in use.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established, actively used open-source project. Repository not fetched during this review; module availability changes frequently as upstream APIs change.

tools.name: Subfinder
tools.summary: Fast passive-only subdomain enumeration from a large set of public and API-based sources.
tools.description:
Subfinder, from ProjectDiscovery, does one thing: enumerate subdomains, passively, quickly. It deliberately does not brute-force or actively probe — it aggregates from certificate transparency, passive DNS, search and threat-intel sources and returns names.

That narrowness is the point. Because it never touches the target, it is the safe default when you have no authorisation to test infrastructure and only want to know what names exist. It is fast enough to run across a large list of domains, which suits mapping an organisation's whole estate or a cluster of related domains.

Limits: passive-only means it finds only what some third party already recorded. Names that were never certificated, never crawled and never seen in passive DNS are invisible to it. It also returns names that no longer resolve.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source under an MIT-style licence. Several of its higher-yield sources require your own API keys; some of those are paid services.
tools.legalNotes: Passive by design — it queries third-party indexes and does not send traffic to the target, which makes it the lowest-risk enumeration option. Standard care applies to what you then do with the discovered hosts.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Reliable within its passive scope and consistent between runs. Recall is bounded by configured sources. Output must be resolved before use — a substantial fraction of returned names are historical and dead.
tools.confidenceNotes: Actively maintained, widely deployed project from an established vendor. Repository not fetched during this review.

tools.name: ZoomEye
tools.summary: China-based internet-wide scanning search engine, useful as a second opinion alongside Shodan and Censys.
tools.description:
ZoomEye indexes hosts, services and web components across the public internet in the same broad category as Shodan and Censys. Its value to an investigator is that it is a different scanner with different vantage points and a different crawl schedule, so it sometimes holds records the others missed — particularly for infrastructure in Asia.

It is used as a corroborating source rather than a primary one: if Shodan, Censys and ZoomEye all show the same certificate on the same host across overlapping windows, that is a much stronger observation than any one of them alone.

Limits and cautions are significant. The operator is subject to Chinese jurisdiction, the interface and documentation are inconsistently translated, and free query allowances are small.
tools.costNotes: A registered free tier with a limited monthly query allowance, plus paid subscription tiers. Specific current allowances and prices were not confirmed in this review.
tools.legalNotes: The operator is subject to Chinese law, including data and cybersecurity legislation that can compel disclosure of user activity to state authorities. Assume your query history is retained and potentially accessible to that jurisdiction. For investigations touching Chinese state interests, dissidents, or sanctioned entities, querying ZoomEye is itself an operational-security decision and should be made deliberately, from an account and network that does not identify you or your subject.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Genuinely useful complementary coverage, but freshness and consistency are less predictable than Shodan or Censys, and documentation gaps make some fields hard to interpret with confidence. Use it to corroborate, not to originate a claim.
tools.confidenceNotes: The service is real and long-running, but current free-tier limits, pricing, and accessibility from outside China were not verified in this review, and access conditions for this class of service have changed before without notice.

tools.name: Maltego
tools.summary: Graph link-analysis platform that runs transforms against many data sources and draws the relationships.
tools.description:
Maltego is the reference tool for visual link analysis in OSINT. You place an entity on a graph — a domain, an email, a person, a company — and run 'transforms' that query data sources and return connected entities, which you then transform in turn. The result is a navigable graph of an investigation rather than a pile of notes.

Its real strength is not any single data source but the accumulation: the graph makes a shared name server, a repeated registrant or a common phone number visible as a shape, which is hard to spot in tabular output. It is widely used in due diligence, fraud investigation and threat intelligence.

The limits are important and often glossed over. A Maltego graph looks authoritative and is not: an edge means 'some data source asserted a connection', which may be stale, wrong, or an artefact of shared infrastructure. Graphs also grow explosively and encourage confirmation bias, because you transform the nodes that support your hypothesis.
tools.costNotes: Maltego Graph Community Edition is free after creating a Maltego ID, offered as Basic (open to everyone) and Basic+ (for qualified users). CE is limited relative to commercial editions — reported limits include up to 10,000 entities per graph, up to 24 results returned per transform, a small monthly allowance of Maltego Data credits, and restricted access to some data modules and connectors. Commercial editions are sold by subscription; many third-party transform hubs are separately paid.
tools.legalNotes: Maltego itself is an analysis client; the legal position depends entirely on which transforms you run. Some transforms perform active queries against targets or third-party services under your API keys, and some data providers in the transform hub have restrictive terms on retention and redistribution. Building a graph about a named private individual creates a personal-data profile with real GDPR consequences — you become the controller of that graph, and it must have a lawful basis, a retention limit and appropriate security.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The tool is dependable; the data is only as good as the transform behind each edge. Maltego does not distinguish visually between a high-confidence and a speculative link, so an unannotated graph systematically overstates certainty. Annotate the provenance of every edge you intend to rely on.
tools.confidenceNotes: Community Edition availability and its Basic / Basic+ structure confirmed during this review against Maltego's own documentation and downloads pages. Specific CE numeric limits are quoted as reported and should be re-checked against the current CE documentation before being relied on.

tools.name: SpiderFoot
tools.summary: Open-source OSINT automation that runs 200-plus modules against a target and correlates the results.
tools.description:
SpiderFoot automates the tedious part of reconnaissance. You give it a seed — a domain, IP, email, name or netblock — choose a scan profile, and it runs a large set of modules against public sources and against each other's output, recursively, until the graph stops growing.

Its value is coverage and repeatability: a SpiderFoot scan reaches sources a human would not think to check, and produces a consistent, exportable record of what was looked at. That auditability matters if your work may be challenged.

The crucial control is the scan profile. SpiderFoot offers passive profiles that only query third-party data, and profiles that actively touch the target. Choosing the wrong one against a sensitive target is a real mistake with legal and operational consequences. Output volume is also very high and heavily weighted toward noise; SpiderFoot finds things, it does not tell you which of them matter.
tools.costNotes: The open-source SpiderFoot is free, self-hosted, and remains actively developed with a version 4 line. A separate commercial hosted product, SpiderFoot HX, has been offered under commercial ownership; its current status and pricing were not confirmed in this review and should not be assumed.
tools.legalNotes: Passive profiles query third-party indexes only. Non-passive profiles resolve, fetch and probe the target and will appear in its logs — treat those as active testing requiring authorisation. Several modules query services under your own API keys, so their terms bind you. A scan seeded with a person's name or email builds a personal-data profile; the resulting database is yours to justify, secure and delete.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Dependable as an automation harness, and self-hosting means no third party sees your targets. Result quality is entirely a function of module configuration and API keys; unconfigured, it returns a fraction of its potential. Correlation output should be read as hypotheses, not findings — false positives are common, particularly on shared hosting and common names.
tools.confidenceNotes: The open-source project was confirmed during this review as actively maintained with a v4 release line, despite one third-party directory listing it as discontinued. The status of the commercial HX offering is explicitly not verified and is flagged as such above.
